newsitem.title: UK: North Sea crude tanker rates soar on vessel shortage.
newsitem.headline: North Sea crude tanker rates soar on vessel shortage.

text.p: Crude oil tanker rates for 80,000 tonne vessels crossing the North Sea have shot up over the past two days due to a dearth of such tonnage for end May loadings, shipping brokers said on Friday.
They said 80,000 tonne vessels were currently offered as high as W180 for North Sea trips, against an average rate of W100-110 seen over the past week.
"Mobil fixed a Statoil vessel from Sture at W155 earlier on and Shell are offering a vessel at W180, but that doesn't mean they'll get it," said one shipping broker.
Elf, meanwhile, was reported to have fixed a vessel at W137.5 out of Sture loading May 28. The Mobil cargo was reported to be loading May 29.
Shipping brokers said that British Petroleum was having trouble finding a suitable vessel for a crude stem.
Oil traders said the dearth of vessels was effecting crude cargo prices in the area.

"Freight rates appear to be soaring and this means offshore loaders will probably firm as well," one trader said referring to offshore loading crudes such as Norway's Gullfaks and Stafjord, and Britain's Beryl which are sold on a delivered basis.
Conversely, fob cargoes could be pressured by the freight rate rises, traders said.

"There are not a lot of cargo vessels available so people have to pay incredibly high freight levels so the only way they are going to lift the crude is if they get a discount on the fob value of it," said one trader.
Shipping brokers atributed the lack of tonnage to the fact that many owners had taken their vessels out of the region due to poor rates over the past few weeks.

"For so long, this market has lagged behind others that a number of owners either fixed or ballasted away, which resulted in a vacuum of available ships," shipping brokers Galbraith's said on their weekly report.
"The short term prospect is for this market to remain high as there are simply fewer vessels available," the report said.

Some shipping brokers and traders noted, however, that the June loading schedules for the eight main British and Norwegian oilfield systems showed a fall of about 260,000 barrels per day against May, which could help alleviate the situation as the market moves into June. -- London Newsroom, +44 171 542 7714.
